content:
Quick answer: Night pain is often what stops sleep with arthritis. Settle the pain side before you chase perfect sleep habits: ask a pharmacist or GP whether your evening pain-relief timing covers the early hours, use heat for stiff aching joints or cold for a hot swollen flare, do gentle range-of-motion before bed, and keep bedclothes light over sore feet. For the full sleep routine, positions and when to ask about CBT for insomnia, use our how to sleep with arthritis guide. Do not change prescribed medicines yourself.

This page is the overnight pain toolkit — what to do in the evening and at night when joints are the reason you cannot settle. It is not a second copy of our sleep-cycle diary guide or the checklist of other causes of broken nights. Use those when you need them:

  • How to sleep with arthritis — the main UK gold-pass sleep guide
  • Poor sleep and arthritis pain — how pain and sleep feed each other, plus a two-week diary
  • Arthritis and sleep problems — what else can keep you awake (medicines, restless legs, sleep apnoea, worry)

Why night pain feels louder

  • Daytime distractions fade, so aching joints get more attention
  • Lying still for hours can leave joints stiffer by morning
  • Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, is often worse overnight and in the early morning — tell your rheumatology team if that pattern is new or fiercer
  • Pain that peaks at 2–4 am is often a clue that your last daytime pain-relief dose has worn off

For wider pain options see our pain relief guide and painkillers and NSAIDs guide.

1. Timing pain relief for the night (with a professional)

  • Ask your pharmacist or GP how long your evening pain relief lasts, and whether a dose closer to bedtime — or a longer-acting option — is suitable for you
  • Some tablets must be taken with food; others can keep you alert if taken late. Get advice for your own list
  • Do not stop, skip or change the dose or timing of prescribed medicines yourself, including steroids, DMARDs or opioids
  • Topical anti-inflammatory gels on knees, hands or feet before bed can help some people when tablets are not enough or not suitable — check with a pharmacist if you take blood thinners or have skin problems

2. Heat and cold before bed

  • Warmth suits dull, stiff, aching joints: a warm bath or shower finishing about an hour before bed, or a microwavable wheat bag wrapped so it cannot burn skin
  • Cold suits a hot, red, swollen flare: an ice pack or bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel for up to about 15–20 minutes
  • Never put ice or a hot pack directly on bare skin, and do not fall asleep on a heat pad

3. Gentle evening movement (not a workout)

Heavy exercise close to bedtime can wind you up. A few minutes of gentle, pain-free range-of-motion — ankle circles, shoulder rolls, easy knee bends on the edge of the bed — can help joints feel less locked when you first lie down. Keep daytime strengthening and walking in your week via the exercise hub; NICE puts exercise at the centre of osteoarthritis care.

4. Take pressure off sore joints in bed

  • Use pillows to support the shape you already find least painful; our sleep positions guide goes joint by joint
  • Keep heavy winter duvets off painful toes and ankles — a light layer, a bed cradle if you have one, or a folded pillow under the covers at the foot of the bed can reduce pressure
  • If turning over wakes you because sheets grip pyjamas, smoother fabrics can help some people; sit carefully on the edge of the bed if sheets are slippery

5. When night pain means the daytime plan needs a review

Pillows and timing help many people. Persistent severe night pain can also mean the underlying arthritis is more active than your current plan covers. See your GP or rheumatology team if:

  • night pain is new, getting worse, or regularly wakes you despite sensible self-care
  • one joint is hot, very swollen and you feel unwell or feverish — seek urgent advice (infection until proven otherwise)
  • morning stiffness lasts much longer than usual, or flares are stacking up — use the flare-up guide and flare action plan

Bring a short note of which joints hurt, what time you wake, and what pain relief you take and when. That helps the appointment more than a vague "I sleep badly".

Frequently asked questions

Should I take painkillers right before sleep?

Sometimes an evening dose closer to bedtime covers the early hours better — but only if your pharmacist or GP says that timing is safe for the medicine you use. Some tablets need food; some can affect sleep or the stomach.

Is heat or cold better for night pain?

Heat often eases stiff, aching joints; cold suits hot swollen flares. If heat makes a joint angrier, switch to cold and seek advice if it does not settle.

Will sleeping tablets fix arthritis night pain?

Sleeping tablets do not treat joint inflammation. They can leave you groggy and are not a long-term plan for pain-driven waking. Fix the pain and sleep-habit sides first, and ask your GP if nights stay poor — see also our sleep and pain cycle guide.
